title: TB5-00294
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Ethiopia, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant), a citizen of Ethiopia, appeals a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) denying his claim for refugee protection.

The Appellant asks that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) set aside the decision of the RPD and determine the Appellant to be a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. In the alternative, the Appellant asks that the RAD set aside the decision of the RPD and refer the matter back to the RPD for re-determination.

The Appellant is relying on new evidence pursuant to Section 110(4), and is requesting an oral hearing pursuant to Section 110(6)1 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA or Act).2 The Minister is not intervening in the appeal.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed. BACKGROUND/ALLEGATIONS

The Appellant alleged that he is an ethnic Somali from XXXX in the Ogaden region of Ethiopia. He stated that there is a group in the Ogaden region known as Ogaden National Liberation Front (ONLF) that fights for freedom from Ethiopia on behalf of the Somalis in Ogaden. He stated that the Ethiopian government has responded by sending special police and many soldiers to the Ogaden region to crush the movement.

In 2004 one of his cousins XXXX XXXX XXXX had joined the ONLF. In XXXX 2005, the Ethiopian soldiers came to his family home and took away his older brother and his sister. Several weeks later, their bodies were found near the military base. In XXXX 2006, his father was detained by the Ethiopian soldiers, and that the family had not seen or heard from his father since that time. In XXXX 2007, his cousin XXXX was raped by the Special Police because they believed that she was a member of the ONLF. XXXX is sister of the Appellant's cousin XXXX XXXX XXXX who was actually a member of the ONLF.

The Appellant alleged that in XXXX 2007, he was arrested and detained by the Secret Police and imprisoned for over two months. Some elders and the Appellant's uncle XXXX negotiated the Appellant's release with the Police on the condition that they would turn in the Appellant's cousin XXXX XXXX XXXX to the Police. Fearing that the Ethiopian Secret Police would kill the Appellant's cousin, the Appellant's uncles XXXX and XXXX told the Appellant that they could not return the Appellant's cousin to the Police. Therefore, they advised the Appellant to run away. The Appellant's uncle kept the Appellant hidden until arrangements were made for him to leave Ethiopia.

The Appellant arrived in Nairobi on XXXX XXXX, 2007. The Appellant did not approach the Kenyan authorities for assistance as he feared that they would return him to Ethiopia. With financial help from his Uncle XXXX, in XXXX 2009, the Appellant engaged a smuggler to go to a safe country. The Appellant left Nairobi on XXXX XXXX, 2009. Travelling through Dubai, Moscow, Cuba, Belize, and Guatemala, the Appellant arrived in Mexico. The Appellant was detained for ten days in Mexico. On XXXX XXXX, 2009, the Appellant made his way to the border of the United States of America (U.S.); upon arrival there, he filed his claim for asylum. His asylum claim was denied. Thereafter, the Appellant crossed the border and entered Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2013. He filed his claim for refugee protection on August 1, 2013.

The Appellant's refugee claim hearing concluded on September 19, 2014. By a decision rendered on December 16, 2014, the RPD rejected the Appellant's claim. The RPD found that the Appellant provided insufficient credible and trustworthy evidence to establish his personal identity, or his identity as a national of Ethiopia of Somali ethnicity, on a balance of probabilities.
The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in its findings on identity. The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in its credibility findings. ADMISSIBILITY OF EVIDENCE SUBMITTED ON APPEAL

The Appellant submits the following five documents3 as new evidence at the RAD: 1. Affidavit of XXXX XXXX XXXX 2. Affidavit of XXXX XXXX XXXX (the Appellant) 3. Letter from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX (XXXX). 4. Appellant's marriage certificate 5. Appellant's school certificate

As provided for in Section 110(3) of the IRPA, with certain exceptions, "...the [RAD] must proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the record of the proceedings of the [RPD], and may accept documentary evidence and written submissions from the Minister and person subject to the appeal...." Section 110(4) of the IRPA indicates that, "the person who is the subject of the appeal may present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection." RAD Rule 3(3)(g)(iii) directs applicants to include an explanation of how the documentary evidence submitted to the RAD meets the requirements of Section 110(4) of the IRPA.

In his affidavit4 and in his Memorandum,5 the Appellant explains why his proposed new evidence should be accepted by the RAD. The RAD reviewed and assessed the Appellant's proposed new evidence, as per Section 110(4) of the IRPA and in the context of the totality of the Appellant's evidence adduced at the RPD, including the recording of the RPD proceedings.

Regarding the affidavit from XXXX XXXX XXXX,6 the RAD finds the Appellant had been in touch with her prior to the rejection of his claim. The Appellant was aware that his identity was an issue at the RPD. The Appellant had not submitted sufficient reliable and satisfactory probative evidence at the RPD in support of his identity. The RAD finds this evidence was reasonably available to the Appellant, and thus the Appellant could reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented the affidavit from XXXX XXXX XXXX at the rejection of his claim. The RAD finds this document does not meet the requirements of Section 110(4) of the IRPA. Therefore, the RAD rejects this evidence.

The RAD finds the Appellant's affidavit, 7 is reiteration of facts that were already before the RPD. Some of the content in the Appellant's affidavit is repetition of what is included in the Appellant's Memorandum of Argument. The RAD finds the Appellant's affidavit does not provide any new information, and thus does not meet the requirements of Section 110(4) of the IRPA. Therefore, the RAD does not accept the Appellant's affidavit as new evidence.

The letter from the XXXX, 8 includes the information that XXXX XXXX XXXX, and XXXX XXXX XXXX who testified at the Appellant's RPD hearing, had communicated to XXXX XXXX, the XXXX XXXX XXXX. The Appellant had met XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX in Canada prior to the rejection of his claim. Therefore, the RAD finds this evidence was reasonably available to the Appellant, and thus the Appellant could reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented information included in this letter at the rejection of his claim. The RAD finds this document does not meet the requirements of Section 110(4) of the IRPA. Therefore, the RAD rejects this evidence.

The Appellant has indicated that after he received the negative determination from the RPD, he made efforts to acquire additional documents in support of his identity. In this respect, the Appellant indicated that the RPD identified the lack of his marriage certificate as one of the reasons for the Appellant's failure to establish his identity; and that he made further efforts to acquire his marriage certificate9 from his wife. The Appellant has submitted his school certificate10 because the RPD had credibility issues arising out of the Appellant's evidence regarding him having attended school in Kenya. Although this evidence was reasonably available to the Appellant prior to the rejection of his claim, based on the above, the RAD finds the Appellant could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented these certificates at the rejection of his claim. Therefore, the RAD finds these documents meet the requirements of Section 110(4) of the IRPA. The RAD accepts these documents.

The Appellant requests that the RAD hold a hearing pursuant to Subsection 110(6) of the Act. Section 110(3) of the IRPA requires that the RAD proceed without a hearing, on the basis of the RPD's record, while allowing the RAD to accept documentary evidence and submissions from the Minister and the Appellant. The person who is the subject of the appeal may, pursuant to Section 110(4), "...present only evidence that arose after the rejection of their claim or that was not reasonably available, or that the person could not reasonably have been expected in the circumstances to have presented, at the time of the rejection." When read together, however, Sections 110(3), (4), and (6) establish that the RAD must not hold a hearing in an appeal unless there is new (Section 110(4)) evidence, in which case the RAD may hold a hearing if that new evidence raises a serious issue with respect to the credibility of the Appellant, is central to the RPD's decision, and that, if accepted, would justify allowing or rejecting the refugee protection claim.

The Appellant has submitted new evidence; the RAD has accepted some of the Appellant's proposed new evidence. The RAD is of the view, even if the Appellant's new documents are reliable and trustworthy, these in and of themselves cannot establish the Appellant's identity relating to he is who he says he is, and that he is national of Ethiopia. The RAD finds the Appellant's new evidence does not meet the test of Section 110(6) because this evidence could not justify allowing or rejecting the claim.
Therefore, the Appellant's request for a hearing is denied.

In assessing the appeal, the RAD is guided by the recent Huruglica11 decision which outlines the approach that the RAD should take as an appellate body in reviewing the first level decisions of the RPD. Justice Phelan has indicated that the RAD conducts a hybrid appeal and is required to review all aspects of the RPD's decision and comes to an independent assessment of whether the Appellant is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. This authority comes from the broad remedial powers of the RAD, including the power to set aside and substitute the RPD's determination that, in its opinion, should have been made as per Subsection 111(1)(b) of the IRPA. The RAD can recognize and respect the conclusions of the RPD on issues such as credibility and/or where the RPD enjoys a particular advantage in reaching its conclusion; however, the RAD has equal or greater expertise to the RPD in the interpretation of country conditions evidence. The RAD is not restricted to intervening on facts where there is a palpable and overriding error. It is not necessary for the RAD to find an error on some standard of review basis in order to trigger its remedial power.

The RAD adopts and applies the Huruglica case law in this appeal. In this regard, the RAD considered the Appellant's submissions,12 and all of the case law submitted.13 MERITS OF THE APPEAL Determination of the Appellant's personal identity and his identity as an Ethiopian citizen

Section 106 of the IRPA states that: The Refugee Protection Division must take into account, with respect to the credibility of a claimant, whether the claimant possesses acceptable documentation establishing identity, and if not, whether they have provided a reasonable explanation for the lack of documentation or have taken reasonable steps to obtain the documentation.

Rule 11 of the RPD Rules states that: The claimant must provide acceptable documents establishing their identity and other elements of the claim. A claimant who does not provide acceptable documents must explain why they did not provide the documents and what steps they took to obtain them.

Further, instructions accompanying the Basis of Claim (BoC) state: You must show the IRB evidence of who you are by giving the IRB official documents with your name and date of birth on them. For example, you can give a passport, national identity card, birth certificate, school certificate, driver's licence, military document, professional or religious membership card. If you do not have documents like this with you, you need to do everything you can to get them immediately. If you still cannot get these documents, you will need to explain the reason for this at your hearing and show that you did everything you could to get them. Attach two copies of all documents (identity, travel or other documents) that you have with you now to support your claim for refugee protection, including documents that are not genuine, documents that you got in an irregular or illegal way or by giving information that is not true, and documents you used that do not really belong to you. In addition to the documents listed above, you can include proof of membership in political organizations, medical or psychological reports, police documents, business records, news clippings, visas, and airplane, train or bus tickets.

In making its determination in this appeal, the RAD considered the totality of the evidence submitted at the RPD, including the recording of the RPD proceedings, and the Appellant's Record, including the New Evidence. The RAD considered the Appellant's medical documents, including the psychiatric assessment provided by Dr. XXXX14 and the medical assessment provided by Dr. XXXX.15

The RPD found that the Appellant provided insufficient credible and trustworthy evidence to establish his personal identity, or his identity as a national of Ethiopia of Somali ethnicity, on a balance of probabilities.16
The Appellant submits that the RPD erred in its findings on identity, and credibility.17.

The RAD assesses the totality of the evidence submitted/adduced in this case, and determines whether the Appellant, on a balance of probabilities, has established his personal identity, and his identity as a national of Ethiopia of Somali ethnicity. Documents submitted at the RPD

The Appellant submitted the following documents in support of his personal identity and his identity as a national of Ethiopia: * Copy of his birth certificate18 * Documents relating to the Appellant's asylum claim in the U.S.19 * Letter from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX20 * Letter from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX21 Copy of the Appellant's birth certificate

Relating to the birth certificate, the RAD finds the Appellant's evidence was inconsistent. The Appellant's explanation for the inconsistencies was that he did not understand the question. In reviewing the recording of the RPD proceedings, the RAD finds the questions asked by the RPD were straightforward. In this regard, the RAD concurs with the RPD's findings that the Appellant's explanation, that he did not understand the questions, for the inconsistencies in his evidence was not satisfactory. Moreover, the RAD finds neither the Appellant nor his counsel raised any issues regarding the ambiguity in questions asked by the RPD. Further, the RPD found that the birth certificate appeared to have been altered. The RAD reviewed the birth certificate, and concurs with the RPD that it appears to have been altered. The Appellant did not know why the birth certificate appeared to have been altered.

Regarding the original birth certificate, the Appellant stated that the original was kept by the authorities in the U.S. The evidence in this case shows that the Appellant came to Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2013. The Appellant testified that he asked his friend to help him after XXXX XXXX, 2014. The Appellant's RPD hearing concluded on September 19, 2014, and the RPD rendered its negative determination on December 16, 2014. The RAD finds the Appellant had sufficient time prior to the conclusion of the Appellant's RPD hearing, and moreover before the rejection of his claim on December 16, 2014, to make a diligent effort to obtain his original birth certificate from the U.S. authorities, if indeed he had submitted it to the U.S. authorities. Moreover, the RPD Rules allow the refugee claimant to make an application to submit documents post-hearing. The RAD finds the Appellant was aware that his personal identity and his identity as an Ethiopian national was an issue at the RPD. The Appellant had not submitted sufficient reliable and trustworthy probative documents to the RPD in support of his personal and national identity. In the circumstance, the RAD finds the Appellant did not demonstrate that he made a reasonable and diligent effort to make inquiries in order to obtain the original of the birth certificate from the U.S. authorities.

The RAD reviewed the Appellant's documents from the U.S. Relating to identity; the U.S. documents state that the identity was established through agency checks and a sworn statement.22 The U.S. documents do not make any mention of the Appellant having submitted an original birth certificate from Ethiopia. Instead the U.S. documents show the following: * Does the individual have valid, government-issued document of identity?23 The response box checked is No (emphasis added).

In reviewing the totality of the evidence in this case, the RAD finds the Appellant provided inconsistent evidence; and further, due to credibility concerns relating to the authenticity of the photocopy-version of the birth certificate and in consideration of the information in the Appellant's U.S. documents, the RAD assigns the photocopy-version of the Appellant's birth certificate little weight in establishing the Appellant's personal identity and his Ethiopian nationality.
Based on the above, the RAD concurs with the RPD in giving the photocopy-version of the Appellant's birth certificate little weight.24 Documents relating to the Appellant's asylum claim in the U.S

The RAD reviewed all of these documents; the RAD finds these documents identify that the Appellant had made an asylum claim in the U.S. The documentation from the U.S. authorities does not unequivocally establish that the Appellant is who he says he is, or that he is a national of Ethiopia. Instead, the U.S. documents indicate that the Appellant had not submitted any valid, government-issued document of identity to the authorities in the U.S. Therefore, the RAD finds these documents in and of themselves, on a balance of probabilities; do not assist the RAD in establishing the Appellant's identity. In this regard, the RAD concurs with the RPD. Letters from XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX

The RAD finds these letters include vague general statements in identifying the Appellant from the XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. These letters do not provide specific details regarding the Appellant's identity as he is who he is, and that he is an Ethiopian national. The RAD gives these documents little weight in establishing the Appellant's identity. In this respect, the RAD concurs with the RPD.25 Testimony of XXXX XXXX XXXX ("witness")

The RAD reviewed the witness testimony and finds the witness was vague in providing details about how she knew the Appellant and how she had known him to be from Ethiopia. The witness testified that she had known the Appellant's family yet she could not provide details about the members of the Appellant's immediate family. The RPD found the witness testimony not to be credible in establishing that the witness knew the Appellant in Ethiopia.26 In reviewing the totality of the evidence in this case, including the witness testimony, the RAD concurs with the RPD in finding that the witness did not establish that she knew the Appellant from Ethiopia. New evidence at the RAD: The Appellant's marriage certificate and his school certificate

The RPD found the Appellant did not provide any reliable and trustworthy probative documentary evidence in support of his personal identity and his identity as a national of Ethiopia. The RAD notes the documents that the Appellant provided at the RPD were all secondary forms of identification, except the photocopy of his birth certificate which the RAD does not find genuine. The Appellant submitted his marriage certificate and his school certificate at the RAD; the RAD accepted these documents. The RAD finds these documents only show that XXXX XXXX XXXX has resided in Kenya in and around the time-period between and around 2008-2009. The RAD acknowledges that the school certificate refers to the Appellant being from Ethiopia; however, the RAD finds this does not establish that the Appellant is an Ethiopian national. Based on the above, the RAD finds the Appellant's marriage certificate and his school certificate from Kenya do not in and of themselves establish that the Appellant is an Ethiopian national. Moreover, these documents do not have any security features, and do not include a photograph of XXXX XXXX XXXX. Therefore, the RAD gives these documents little weight in assessing the Appellant's personal identity and his identity as a national of Ethiopia. The Appellant's psychiatric report

The Appellant submits that the Immigration and Refugee Board (Board) placed limited weight on his psychiatric assessment because the panel could not conclude that the diagnosis of (Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder) PTSD was a result of the circumstances alleged by the Appellant.27 The RAD finds the RPD assessed28 the Appellant's psychiatric assessment provided by Dr. XXXX29 and his medical assessment30 provided by Dr. XXXX, both affiliated with the Canadian Centre for Victims of Torture, in the context of the totality of the evidence submitted/adduced at the RPD. The RAD finds the RPD noted that the Appellant's testimony was inconsistent with the information that the Appellant had provided to Dr. XXXX.31 Regardless, given the credibility concerns with the Appellant's evidence, the RAD finds the Appellant's psychiatric report did not overcome the shortcomings in the Appellant's evidence. In this case, the RAD finds the comments of the Court in Danailov32 to be particularly relevant, specifically that "opinion evidence is only as valid as the truth of the facts on which it is based." As noted by the Federal Court in Rokni,33 a report of this kind "cannot possibly serve as a cure-all for any and all deficiencies in the claimant's testimony." The RAD finds the Appellant's argument that the Board placed limited weight on his psychiatric assessment because the panel could not conclude that the diagnosis of PTSD was a result of the circumstances alleged by the Appellant is without merit.

Regarding identity, the RAD finds the evidence in this case shows that the Appellant initially submitted secondary forms of identity documents at the RPD, and subsequently made efforts to obtain additional documents to support his personal identity as XXXX XXXX XXXX, and that he is an Ethiopian national. In this case, however, the RAD finds the determinative issue is whether the totality of the Appellant's evidence submitted, on a balance of probabilities, establishes the Appellant's personal identity as XXXX XXXX XXXX, and his identity as a national of Ethiopia.

Based on the totality of the evidence adduced in this case, the RAD finds the Appellant, on a balance of probabilities, has failed to provide sufficient reliable and trustworthy probative evidence to establish his personal identity, he is who he says he is, and that he is an Ethiopian national.

The RAD is aware that sometimes the refugee claimants cannot provide authentic probative identity documents. In the presence of credibility concerns, however, as in this case, it was open to the RPD to look for more reliable and satisfactory probative documents to establish that the Appellant is who he says he is, and that he is an Ethiopian national.

Based on the foregoing analysis and reasons, the RAD finds the Appellant has not provided sufficient reliable and satisfactory probative evidence to establish his identity as to he is who he says he is. The RAD finds the Appellant has failed to establish with credible and trustworthy probative evidence, on a balance of probabilities, that he is who he says he is. Therefore, the RAD concurs with the RPD in that the Appellant has not, on a balance of probabilities, established his personal identity as XXXX XXXX XXXX, and that he is a national of Ethiopia. Determination of the Appellant's claim for refugee protection

The RPD completed an assessment of the Appellant's alleged risk upon return to Ethiopia. In this respect, the RAD finds the Appellant has failed to establish with credible and trustworthy probative evidence, on a balance of probabilities, that he is who he says he is. Therefore, the RAD cannot establish who the Appellant is. As such, the RAD cannot find the Appellant to be a Convention refugee or a person in need of Canada's protection. The RAD is bound by the jurisprudence of the Court. Justice Blanchard noted in Ipala,34 "The decisions of this Court clearly indicate that a refugee claim must be dismissed once the Board determines that the identity of the claimant has not been proven."35 Justice Blanchard in Ipala,36 citing Justice Beaudry's reasoning in Najam37 stated, "The proof of a claimant's identity is of central importance to his or her claim. ...[I]f the identity of the claimant is not proven, the claim must fail; that means the Board need not pursue an analysis of the evidence in relation to other aspects of the claim." In this respect, the RAD concurs with the RPD.
Based on the foregoing analysis and reasons, this appeal fails.

Pursuant to Section 111(1)(a) of the IRPA, the RAD confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. This appeal is dismissed.
